title: Patrol Y61 (GU)
eyebrow: NISSAN PATROL · Y61 'GU' · 1997–2016 (LATER IN SOME MARKETS)
verdict: The GU is the Patrol that kept the solid axles and coils of the GQ, added a squarer body and spent nineteen years in Australian showrooms. Buy the right engine and it's one of the great touring wagons. Buy an early ZD30 without paperwork and you might be buying a set of pistons.

paragraphs: In December 1997 Nissan replaced the [[nissan-patrol/y60|Y60 'GQ']] with a Patrol that looked new but thought the same way. The Y61, sold as the GU in Australia and the Safari in Japan, kept a separate chassis, coil springs and a live axle at each end on the wagon, at a time when Toyota was giving the [[land-cruiser/100-series|100 Series]] independent front suspension. Nissan Australia sold 104,510 GU wagons and 37,112 cab-chassis between 1997 and October 2016, and some markets kept building it until 2024. Few 4x4s have had a run that long.

story.heading: SAME RECIPE, SQUARER BOX
paragraphs: Underneath, the GU is an evolution of the GQ. Wikipedia notes larger CV joints, manual gearboxes with fewer synchros, and wider axle housings to suit the new body, with the same H233 and H260 differential centres. The wagon rides on a 2,970 mm wheelbase. Body styles were the seven-seat wagon, a cab-chassis (the UY61 in Australia), sold with either a leaf-sprung or a coil-sprung rear, and a two-door pickup. Japan also got a two-door hardtop and a four-door van.

The engine list at launch covered every taste. Australian Series I trucks offered the 4.5-litre TB45E petrol six, the 2.8-litre RD28ETi turbo-diesel six, and the 4.2-litre TD42 diesel. The TD42T turbo-diesel joined the ST in 1999. CarsGuide notes that the RD28 had a timing belt, the TD42 timing gears, and the ZD30 and petrol sixes chains. Manuals were five-speeds: the FS5R30A behind the RD28 and the FS5R50B behind everything else.

story.heading: THE ZD30 PROBLEM
paragraphs: Series II arrived in 2000 with the engine that defines the GU's reputation: the 3.0-litre ZD30DDTi, a four-cylinder turbo-diesel with a Bosch VP44 pump, rated at 116 kW. It was cheaper than the 4.2 six and could be had with an automatic. CarsGuide's David Morley writes that it was remembered 'neither for those attributes nor remotely fondly'. Too many engines died early, usually through a holed crown or a cracked ring land on the number three or four piston, and the fix was a bottom-end rebuild.

Nobody has published a definitive cause. The suspects are the EGR system upsetting the mixture and creating hot spots, oil from the crankcase vent fouling the mass-airflow sensor, and boost spikes from a slow-reacting turbo control. Nissan also originally specified 6 litres of oil. After reports of oil starvation it raised the capacity to 8.3 litres and told dealers to shorten and recalibrate the dipsticks. Owners responded with what forums call 'engine saver' mods: boost and EGT gauges, catch cans, and in many cases a blanked EGR.

story.heading: SERIES BY SERIES
paragraphs: Series III, from late 2001, brought the 4.8-litre TB48DE petrol six, a DOHC 24-valve engine rated at 185 kW in Australia, and later the intercooled TD42Ti. The 2003 Japanese facelift is credited to Junichi Sakai. The big visual change came with Series IV in late 2004: boxy wheel-arch flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, and five-spoke 17-inch alloys. Nissan Australia described it as a major facelift with no mechanical changes.

In 2007 the TD42 was dropped because it couldn't meet Euro IV, and a common-rail ZD30 became the only wagon diesel, at 118 kW and up to 380 Nm. CarsGuide suggests that the common-rail system may have helped with the boost and mixture problems. Dual front airbags only became standard across the range that year. By the end in Australia, the 3.0 was the only engine left.

story.heading: THE LONG GOODBYE
paragraphs: The petrol-only Y62 reached Australia in 2013, so the GU stayed on sale beside it until 2016. It finished with the 300-unit Legend Edition: an ST with the common-rail 3.0, a rear differential lock, a bull bar, a winch and a snorkel. Because the newer truck had no diesel, late GUs held their value. Wikipedia lists a worldwide phase-out in 2014, but sales continued in South Africa, the Middle East and parts of Africa, Asia and South America. Production finally ended in 2024.

Its rivals were Toyota's IFS 100 Series and its solid-axle [[land-cruiser/100-series|105]], with the [[land-cruiser/70-series|70 Series]] as the cab-chassis alternative. The GU's case is simple: coil-sprung solid axles, a huge aftermarket and a truck that UN agencies and armies still drive. Pick the engine carefully and it can last for decades.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE DESERT PATROL
callout.title: Super Safari: the Y61 that refused to retire
paragraphs: Outside Australia the Y61 lived on as the Patrol Safari and Super Safari, built in Japan until 2024 for markets such as the Gulf. A 2017 Middle East brochure lists the TB48DE at 280 hp (SAE gross), a five-speed automatic, a rear differential lock, VDC, an electric winch and tan leather. Wikipedia notes that the TB48DE has a following among Middle Eastern tuners, and that the Gulf had special editions with names like Falcon, Gazelle and Al Ostoura.

Japan's version was the Safari, and it took a different route: the 245 PS TB48DE in the Granroad Limited from November 2002, and a rear limited-slip diff on every model from September 1999. The Safari name disappeared from Japanese showrooms in the mid-2000s, while the Gulf trucks kept going for most of another twenty years.

engineering_intro: The GU is a traditional ladder-frame 4x4 with a beam axle and coil springs at each end on the wagon. The front axle is located by radius arms and a panhard rod, which is why lifted GUs need caster correction. Drive is part-time 4WD with low range and auto-locking free-wheel hubs as standard on many trucks. The engine range is the main thing that separates good GUs from expensive ones.

engineering.note: Wagon, UY61 cab-chassis and two-door pickup. Cab-chassis trucks came with either leaf or coil rear suspension.
Radius arms and a panhard rod at the front. Lifts of about 2 in or more usually need caster-correction bushes. Series 4 and later panhard rods differ from earlier ones.
Wider housings than the GQ, with the same centres. Some GUs have an H233B rear and some an H260, so check before you buy a locker.
Selected mechanically. Auto-locking hubs can unlock when you rock a stuck truck, so many owners fit manual hubs. The Legend Edition's low range is 2.02:1.

engineering.v: TB45E / TB48DE petrol; RD28ETi, ZD30DDTi, TD42 / TD42T / TD42Ti diesel
engineering.note: Output ranged from 91 kW for the non-turbo TD42 to 185 kW for the TB48 (Australian figures).

engineering.v: FS5R30A / FS5R50B manual; RE4R03A 4-sp / RE5R05A 5-sp auto
engineering.note: The four-speed auto was offered with the TB45 and ZD30, and the five-speed auto with the TB48.

generations_table.engine: TB45E 4.5 petrol · RD28ETi 2.8 TD · TD42 4.2 D · TD42T (from 1999)
generations_table.note: Australian launch range. RD28 was manual only.
Automatic available. Non-turbo TD42 dropped from wagons. This is the ZD30 era to check most carefully.
ST-L added in 2003. TD42Ti offered on every variant except the Ti.
Facelift with box flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, and 17-in five-spoke alloys. No mechanical changes. TB48 became Euro III and auto-only in 2006.
TD42 dropped because it couldn't meet Euro IV. Dual airbags standard from 2007. Ended with the 300-unit Legend Edition.
Built in Japan until 2024. Rear diff lock on the Super Safari.

buying_checks.head: Identify the engine and series first
buying_checks.body: Make sure the engine and gearbox match the build date and series. A 'Series III ZD30' and a 'Series IV TB48' are different buys. A ZD30 sold as 'overhauled' should come with an itemised list: head, bores, pistons, bearings and rings, not just new pistons and a turbo.

buying_checks.head: ZD30: demand oil history and check the dipstick
buying_checks.body: Look for regular oil changes and the right grade. Nissan Australia specifies 10W-40 ACEA B3 at no more than 10,000 km or 6 months. Fuel in the oil is bad news. One forum veteran says heavy soot within 5,000 km points to an open EGR. Check the intercooler for oil staining and listen for knocks on a cold start.

buying_checks.head: Cooling under load
buying_checks.body: Every GU engine can overheat when towing, and the TD42 has a particular reputation for it. Check the radiator core, the foam seals between condenser and radiator, and the fan clutch (it should drag and turn only about half a revolution when cold). Watch the temperature gauge on a long climb.

buying_checks.head: Manual gearbox
buying_checks.body: Drive through every gear. Owners report fifth-gear spline and hub problems and worn 2nd-to-3rd synchros on the five-speed.

buying_checks.head: Rear axle seals, diffs and underbody
buying_checks.body: Put it on a hoist. Look for wet rear backing plates from leaking axle seals, bash plates pushed up into what they're meant to protect, and damage to sills and bumpers. Find out whether the rear diff is an H233B or an H260 if you plan to fit a locker.

buying_checks.head: Cab-chassis: look behind the cab
buying_checks.body: ExplorOz members report cracks in GU cab-chassis frames just behind the cab and near the rear axle on heavily loaded trays, repaired by plating. Check under any big service body.

buying_checks.head: Rear barn door and dash
buying_checks.body: Check the big rear door that carries the spare for cracks down the side of the window on the left-hand side. Dashboard tops can blister or bubble.

buying_checks.head: Previous lift work
buying_checks.body: A lifted GU that wanders or steers vaguely probably needs caster correction. Lifts of about 3 in or more also need longer panhard rods, drag-link changes and longer brake lines. Ask what was fitted and whether it was certified.

repairs.title: ZD30 'engine saver' setup (gauges, oil level, breather)
repairs.time: ≈ Half a day to a day
repairs.symptoms: None until a piston fails, usually number three or four. Warning signs include high EGTs when towing, boost spikes or drops under load, sooty oil, and oil consumption.
repairs.fix: Make sure the dipstick and service fill reflect Nissan's revised 8.3-litre capacity, then check the oil daily on hard trips. Fit a boost gauge and a pyrometer (EGT gauge) and learn what's normal. One owner saw 300–450 °C at highway speed with the EGR working and about 600 °C on a steep climb at full throttle. Back off before EGTs climb. Fit a catch can so crankcase oil doesn't reach the intake and MAF sensor, and keep the MAF clean. Blanking the EGR is common but disputed: one owner saw lower highway boost and higher EGTs after blanking it and refitted the valve. It is also an emissions device, so check your local rules.
repairs.tools: Pyrometer probe drilled into the exhaust manifold (pre-turbo) · boost gauge tee into the intake · catch can kit · MAF cleaner

repairs.title: Front wheel bearing service and hub seals
repairs.symptoms: Play in the wheel when rocked top to bottom, grinding, grease on the inside of the rim, or an auto hub that runs hot after a drive.
repairs.fix: Put the axle on stands and remove the wheel. Set the auto-locking hub to LOCK, remove its six 8 mm Allen bolts and pull the hub. Undo the two 22 mm caliper (torque member) bolts and tie the caliper out of the way. Remove the snap ring, washer and thrust ring, the lock-washer screws and lock washer, then the bearing lock nut. Pull the hub, catching the outer bearing, then lever out the seal and remove the inner bearing. Clean and repack both bearings, and fit a new seal. On reassembly, the Gregory's manual quoted on ExplorOz says to torque the lock nut to 167–196 Nm while rotating the hub, back it off, retighten to 3–5 Nm, then check the preload with a spring gauge (0–18.6 N starting force). A Lonard's procedure gives different figures, so confirm the spec in a workshop manual.
repairs.tools: 8 mm Allen key · 22 mm socket and breaker bar · GU hub-nut socket · circlip pliers · seal driver (the old seal flipped over works) · wheel-bearing grease · spring gauge

parts.name: Front wheel bearing kits for Patrol GU

repairs.title: Cure overheating under load (TD42 and others)
repairs.symptoms: Temperature gauge climbs when towing or climbing in fifth gear on hot days, and the A/C cuts out because of the radiator temperature sensor.
repairs.fix: Clean the radiator core thoroughly. Owners note that blocked internal tubes won't clear with a flush, so a recore or new radiator may be needed. Refit or replace the foam seals between the condenser and radiator so air can't bypass the core. Check the viscous fan clutch: when cold it should drag and spin only about half a turn. Check that the underbody air dam and wheel-well rubbers are in place, especially on lifted trucks. Fit a new thermostat and coolant at the correct mix. Fit an EGT gauge and drive by it: drop from fifth to fourth when towing and ease off at around 450–500 °C.
repairs.tools: Radiator brushes and fin comb · coolant pressure tester · EGT gauge

repairs.title: Caster correction after a lift
repairs.time: ≈ Half a day (bushes) to a full day (arms)
repairs.symptoms: Light, wandering steering that won't self-centre after a suspension lift.
repairs.fix: Lifting a radius-arm front axle rotates it and reduces caster. One owner with a nominal 2 in kit (closer to 3 in in practice) fitted 2° caster-correction bushes and reported a clear improvement. Press the old radius-arm bushes out at the chassis end and press in offset bushes, set to add caster. For lifts of about 3 in or more, forum members also recommend an adjustable or longer panhard rod to re-centre the axle, drag-link changes and longer brake lines. Get a wheel alignment afterwards. Series 4 and later panhard rods differ from earlier ones, so order for your series.
repairs.tools: Bush press or a shop press · jacks and stands · alignment afterwards

repairs.title: Rear axle seal and bearing leak
repairs.symptoms: Wet backing plate or inner rim, oily brake shoes or pads, a falling diff oil level.
repairs.fix: Rear axle oil seals are a known GU leak. Drain or lower the diff oil, remove the wheel and brake, and undo the axle retainer. Pull the axle with a slide hammer, then replace the inner oil seal in the housing. If the bearing is rough, have the bearing and collar pressed off and on at a shop. Clean contaminated brake parts or replace them, refit the axle and refill with LSD-rated gear oil if the diff is a limited-slip.
repairs.tools: Slide hammer · seal puller and driver · access to a press · brake cleaner

parts.name: Rear wheel bearing kit, drum-brake Patrol GU (cab-chassis)

repairs.title: Fit a rear locker
repairs.symptoms: Not a fault. The rear LSD on many GUs isn't enough on rocky climbs and cross-axle ruts.
repairs.fix: First find out which rear diff you have. Harrop's GU ELocker and the Detroit H233 unit suit the H233B only, and the GU used both H233B and H260 rear centres. Remove the axles and carrier, swap the ring gear onto the locker, and fit new carrier bearings. Set preload and backlash and check the tooth pattern before refilling. Air lockers need a compressor and air line, and electric lockers need wiring to a dash switch. Shops usually do this, because a bad setup ruins the ring and pinion.
repairs.tools: Bearing puller and press · dial indicator · inch-pound torque wrench · marking compound

parts.name: Harrop ELocker, Patrol GU-GQ rear, 33 spline (GU: H233B rear only)
Detroit Locker, Patrol rear H233, 33 spline
Terrain Tamer diff bearing kit TTEL10 (GU/GQ H233B front and rear)

repairs.title: Swap auto-locking hubs for manual hubs
repairs.symptoms: Front drive drops out when you rock a stuck truck back and forth. CarsGuide notes this is a known trait of the auto hubs.
repairs.fix: With the axle on stands, remove the six Allen bolts holding each auto hub (as in the bearing service above), pull the hub assembly and fit the manual hub kit according to its instructions. Check the bearing preload while you're there. Run both hubs in LOCK whenever you're in 4WD.
repairs.tools: 8 mm Allen key · circlip pliers · grease

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: Forum owners commonly run 285/75R16 (about 33 in) on 16-inch rims on a stock-height GU. One owner runs 305/70R16 on a 2004 GU with only a 'tiny' scrub at full lock in reverse. Bigger sizes such as 305/70R17 and 35s are generally reported with at least a 2 in lift and the mud flaps removed. Many GUs won't take 15-inch rims over their brakes. In Australia the usual limit without engineering is 50 mm larger in overall diameter than the placard tyre.

CarsGuide's used-buyer advice favours the 4.2 diesel and the petrol sixes and urges caution with the RD28 and the ZD30, especially high-mileage bush trucks. Owners describe the TD42T as 'ultra reliable' if it's kept cool and full of oil, and the TB48 as strong and reliable but thirsty. The RD28 is known for injection-pump failures and blown head gaskets.

faq.q: Is the ZD30 really that bad, and which years were fixed?
faq.a: Nobody agrees on a cut-off and no failure rate has been published. Typical failures are a holed or cracked number three or four piston. Nissan raised the oil capacity to 8.3 L and recalibrated the dipsticks. One forum veteran says most bugs were ironed out by 2003, while others point to the 2007-on common-rail engine. Many high-mileage ZD30s run fine. Buy on service history and condition, not on the year alone.

faq.q: Should I blank the EGR on a ZD30?
faq.a: It's the most argued-about ZD30 mod. Some owners blank it to keep soot out of the intake and report quicker spool. Others have seen highway boost drop and EGTs rise after blanking it, and refitted it. If you do it, fit boost and EGT gauges so you can see the effect. The EGR is an emissions control device, so check your local roadworthiness rules.

faq.q: How much can a GU tow?
faq.a: CarsGuide lists braked towing limits of 3,500 kg for the 4.2 turbo-diesel and 4.8 petrol wagons, 3,200 kg for the 3.0 diesel wagon, 3,140 kg for the 4.5 petrol, 2,800 kg for the 2.8 diesel, and up to 2,500 kg for the cab-chassis and ute, all with a suitable heavy-duty towbar. The 2016 Legend Edition is rated at 3,200 kg as a manual and 2,500 kg as an auto.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Nissan Australia quotes 17.2 L/100 km (ADR combined) for the 4.8-litre petrol. A 2010 common-rail ZD30 DX cab-chassis is listed at 12.5 L/100 km combined (15.9 urban, 10.5 highway). A loaded touring truck on big tyres will use more.

Japanese Safaris had a rear LSD as standard from September 1999, and later Australian cab-chassis list an LSD as standard. A factory rear diff lock is documented on the 2016 Legend Edition and the Middle East Super Safari. For everything else, ARB Air Lockers, Harrop ELockers and Detroits are the usual upgrades. Check whether your rear diff is an H233B or an H260 before you order.

faq.q: What oil does a ZD30 take, and how much?
faq.a: Nissan Australia specifies 10W-40 to ACEA B3, changed at least every 10,000 km or 6 months. The capacity was raised from 6 L to 8.3 L, and dealers recalibrated the dipsticks. Make sure yours has been done and fill to the revised mark. A Nissan representative quoted on ExplorOz advised using 9 L at changes and checking the oil daily when working hard.

faq.q: How do I tell the series apart?
faq.a: Series I–III (1997–2004) have the original smooth arches and smaller tail-lights. The late-2004 Series IV facelift added box-style flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, and 17-inch five-spoke alloys. A diesel GU wagon built from 2007 has the common-rail ZD30, because the TD42 was dropped that year.

faq.q: Can I import one to the US or Canada?
faq.a: The US 25-year exemption counts from each vehicle's month of manufacture, so early GUs from 1997 to 2001 are now eligible. EPA rules also require the original engine configuration or a certified replacement. Canada's limit is 15 years. Bring a Trailer has sold several Y61-era Safaris and Patrols.

faq.q: Why does the front drive drop out when I'm stuck?
faq.a: The auto-locking free-wheel hubs can disengage when you rock the truck back and forth to get unstuck. That's why many owners fit manual hub kits. Engage 4WD with the truck stationary and in neutral, because the GU's 4WD selection is mechanical.

mods.why: A 2 in lift with new coils and shocks clears 33s and makes up for touring weight. Plan for caster correction on the radius-arm front axle.
Offset radius-arm bushes restore caster, and an adjustable panhard rod re-centres the axle on taller lifts.
The factory LSD gives up on cross-axle climbs. A rear locker is the biggest single traction upgrade, and a front one for serious rock work.
Boost and EGT gauges are what owners use to keep a ZD30 or a towing TD42 alive.
The GU is a touring truck, so bull bars, winches, rock sliders, roof racks and drawers all have a big aftermarket.

baseline_service.intro: Assume nothing has been done without receipts. On a GU, the job that matters most depends on the engine. A ZD30 needs proof of frequent oil changes and the revised oil level. A TD42 needs a cooling system that can cope with towing. Every GU needs the diff, transfer and hub servicing that bush trucks skip. Driveline capacities below are handbook figures quoted by an owner. Check them against your manual, since they vary by engine and body.

items.spec: ZD30: 10W-40 ACEA B3, revised capacity 8.3 L. TB48: owner's manual says 5W-30. Other engines: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.interval: ZD30: at least every 10,000 km or 6 months. Many owners go shorter when towing
items.note: On a ZD30, confirm the dipstick has been recalibrated to the revised capacity. Sludge or grit under a cold oil filler cap is a bad sign.

items.spec: Dry element, [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] part number
items.interval: Inspect at every service, more often in dust
items.note: On the ZD30, oil on the MAF sensor (from crankcase venting or an over-oiled aftermarket filter) is a suspected cause of bad fuelling. Clean it with MAF cleaner and consider a catch can.

items.interval: Replace at purchase, then per the schedule
items.note: Early ZD30s are known for fuel-pump and fuel-system trouble (the Bosch VP44 pump), and clean fuel is cheap insurance.

items.interval: Test if cold starts are slow
items.note: Worn glow plugs are a common cause of hard starting on older diesels.

items.spec: RD28: belt. ZD30 and TB45/TB48: chain. TD42: gears
items.interval: RD28 belt: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Replace if there's no record
items.note: Only the 2.8 RD28 has a belt to budget for.
Clean the core, refit the condenser foam seals and check the fan clutch (about half a turn when cold). This matters most on a TD42 that tows.

items.spec: ≈ 3.8 L (handbook figure quoted on ExplorOz). Grade: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: Check the fifth gear and the 2nd-to-3rd shift while you're under there. Both are known weak spots.

items.spec: ≈ 3–4 L drains from the pan, about 12 L total (2001 ZD30 owner). ATF type: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.interval: One owner cites Nissan at 40,000 km for ATF
items.note: A pan drain changes only about a third of the fluid. Do several drain-and-fills, or have a transmission shop exchange it through the cooler line (about 16 L).

items.spec: ≈ 1.9 L (handbook figure, and also quoted by a 2001 ZD30 owner as Dexron III). [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] for your gearbox
items.note: Fluid type differs by model, so check the manual or the tag before filling.

items.spec: Front axle ≈ 5.4 L, rear ≈ 2.1 L (handbook figures quoted on ExplorOz). The rear is commonly an LSD and needs LSD-rated gear oil
items.interval: Change at purchase and after deep water crossings
items.note: CarsGuide says hard-used GUs need regular diff oil changes. Note whether your rear is an H233B or an H260.

items.spec: Repack with wheel-bearing grease. Set the preload to the workshop manual figure
items.interval: At purchase, then about every 40,000 km or after water crossings
items.note: CarsGuide also recommends lubricating the front swivel joints on hard-used trucks. Auto hubs should be warm, not hot, after a drive.

items.note: Check for gear oil on the rear brakes from leaking axle seals, and that the calipers clear your wheels. Caliper sizes vary by year.
